TABS.label: For the kids
TABS.title: For the kids
TABS.lede: A page written for them. Simple words, big letters.

hurt.label: I'm in the hospital or can't communicate

steps.t: Make sure you and the kids are safe
steps.d: Call 911 if anyone is in danger. It's okay to let someone else drive or make calls for you.

steps.t: Arrange care for the kids
steps.d: Call the person listed for school pickup and overnight care. Use the safe word.

steps.t: Bring my medical papers to the hospital
steps.d: My healthcare directive and medical power of attorney let you speak for me. Bring my insurance card, ID, and medication list.

steps.t: Start a call log
steps.d: Write down who you talked to, when, and what they said. Hospitals and insurers will ask.

steps.t: Call my employer's HR
steps.d: Ask about sick leave, short‑term disability, FMLA job protection, and how my paycheck continues.

steps.t: Check that bills are still on autopay
steps.d: Nothing needs to change right away. Look over the bills list so nothing is missed.

steps.t: Pick one person to share updates
steps.d: They tell everyone else, so you're not repeating hard news.

steps.t: Use the financial power of attorney if needed
steps.d: If you need to manage accounts only in my name, this document lets you act for me. Call our attorney if a bank pushes back.

steps.t: File disability or insurance claims
steps.d: Check my disability and any accident or critical‑illness policies.

steps.t: Ask the hospital for a social worker
steps.d: They help with insurance questions, rehab placement, and paperwork. It's a free service.

steps.t: Let yourself stop
steps.d: You don't have to decide anything big today. Call the first person on the list and let them help.

steps.t: Arrange care for the kids
steps.d: Ask someone they trust to be with them. There's a page written for them.

steps.t: Read my wishes
steps.d: My preferences for a funeral, burial or cremation, and a service are written down.

steps.t: Contact the funeral home
steps.d: They help with arrangements and ordering death certificates. Ask for 10 to 15 certified copies; banks and insurers each want one.

steps.t: Call my employer's HR
steps.d: Ask about final pay, group life insurance, retirement accounts, and health coverage for you and the kids.

steps.t: Keep the home running
steps.d: Keep paying the mortgage or rent, insurance, and utilities. Keep joint checking open so final paychecks or reimbursements can be deposited; solo accounts may freeze when notified.

steps.t: Keep my phone charged and on
steps.d: Many accounts send login codes to it. Don't cancel the line yet.

steps.t: Call our estate attorney
steps.d: They'll walk you through the will or trust and what happens next. Bring the will.

steps.t: File life insurance claims
steps.d: Each policy needs a claim form and a death certificate.

steps.t: Don't rush to pay solo unsecured debts
steps.d: Credit cards and medical bills solely in my name belong to the estate, not you personally. Keep paying joint bills and essentials, and ask our attorney before paying solo debts.

steps.t: Contact Social Security
steps.d: You and the kids may be eligible for survivor benefits. Call 1‑800‑772‑1213.

steps.t: Get help with accounts and taxes
steps.d: Our financial advisor and accountant can help move accounts and plan the tax return.

steps.t: Protect my identity
steps.d: Send a death certificate to Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion so no one opens credit in my name.

steps.t: Retitle the house and cars
steps.d: Our attorney can tell you what's needed for each.

steps.t: Cancel my subscriptions and memberships
steps.d: Use the list so nothing keeps charging.

steps.t: Update your own beneficiaries and will
steps.d: Your accounts probably name me. Update them when you're ready.

steps.t: Hold off on big decisions
steps.d: Selling the house, moving, or large money choices can wait several months. Grief support helps; you don't have to do this alone.

steps.t: Know your runway
steps.d: Compare emergency savings to our monthly spending. That's how many months you have.

steps.t: File for unemployment
steps.d: Apply with the state right away if a job ended; benefits usually start from the date you file.

steps.t: Sort out health insurance
steps.d: Ask about COBRA (you usually have 60 days to elect it) and compare marketplace plans.

steps.t: Trim to the essentials
steps.d: Housing, food, utilities, insurance, minimum debt payments. Pause the rest.

steps.t: Call lenders before you miss a payment
steps.d: Ask about hardship programs. They're more flexible when you call early.

steps.t: Avoid cashing out retirement
steps.d: Early withdrawals usually come with taxes and penalties. Talk to our advisor first.

steps.t: Make sure everyone is safe
steps.d: If there's a medical or safety emergency, call 911 and read our home address from the kids page.

steps.t: Call our first emergency contact
steps.d: Let a trusted local adult know where we are and ask them to come over or coordinate.

steps.t: Reassure the kids
steps.d: Use our safe word so they know you're a trusted helper, and stick to their comfort routine.

steps.t: Find medical consent and guardian papers
steps.d: Hospitals need a signed medical consent or temporary guardian letter before treating the kids.

steps.t: Check allergies, medications, and school pickup
steps.d: Review everyone's medical details and let the school know who is picking up.

steps.t: Take care of pets and the house
steps.d: Check feeding schedules, medications, and alarm/key notes.

steps.t: Notify our estate attorney and backup guardian
steps.d: They can step in with legal authority if both of us are incapacitated.

steps.t: Keep a log of calls and decisions
steps.d: Note who you spoke with, medical updates, and expenses.

visa.label: Work visa / cross-border emergency (H-1B, NRI, Expat)

steps.t: Check dependent visa status & grace-period clock
steps.d: If a primary visa holder (e.g., H-1B, L-1, Skilled Worker) passes away or loses employment, dependents (e.g., H-4, L-2) can face an immediate status change or 60-day clock. Contact an immigration attorney before leaving the country.

steps.t: Secure passports, visa papers & kids' temporary care
steps.d: Locate I-797/I-94/I-140, passports, EADs, and OCI/residency cards. If both parents are incapacitated, call the local temporary guardian right away so kids stay with trusted adults while overseas family arranges visas.

steps.t: Contact the home-country Embassy or Consulate if needed
steps.d: Embassies assist with emergency travel documents, repatriation of remains, and notarized cross-border letters.

steps.t: Call employer HR & company immigration counsel
steps.d: Request copies of all immigration filings (I-140, PERM, I-485, I-797) and ask about survivor relief (e.g., INA § 204(l)), final pay, and group life insurance.

steps.t: Check both host-country and home-country wills
steps.d: Cross-border families often have separate wills for each country. Confirm neither revokes the other, and ask a cross-border attorney about non-citizen estate tax rules (e.g., $60k NRA threshold in the US) before moving assets.

steps.t: Map overseas accounts, nominees & property
steps.d: List NRE/NRO/FCNR, Demat, EPF/PPF, foreign bank accounts, and property. Note that in countries like India, a bank/demat nominee is often only a custodian—legal heirs/will govern final ownership.

steps.t: Keep a 1-page ER & Medical Grab Sheet ready
steps.d: Record exact diagnosis, active protocol, allergies, implants/ports/lines, red-flag thresholds, 24/7 specialist triage line, and preferred hospital/ER.
steps.ref: Health → Chronic / critical illness & ER care

steps.t: Set up patient portal proxy & HIPAA / medical release
steps.d: Enable caregiver proxy access on MyChart/hospital portals and sign medical release forms so doctors and insurers can legally talk to your spouse or advocate.
steps.ref: Health → Chronic / critical illness & ER care

steps.t: Check Critical Illness, Hospital Indemnity, Disability & FMLA
steps.d: A major diagnosis often triggers lump-sum Critical Illness or Hospital Indemnity payouts, plus Short/Long-Term Disability and intermittent FMLA for both patient and caregiving spouse.

phases.when: 2 AM ER trip or sudden flare-up

steps.t: Follow the specialist's red-flag rule first
steps.d: Check exact fever, blood pressure, oxygen, or glucose thresholds and call the 24/7 specialist triage line BEFORE taking fever-reducers (which can mask a dangerous infection) or going to an unlinked ER.
steps.ref: Health → Chronic / critical illness & ER care

steps.t: Alert triage immediately about implants, ports, lines & arm limits
steps.d: Point out port-a-cath, PICC line, pacemaker/ICD, dialysis fistula, insulin pump, or lymphedema arm restrictions (no blood pressure cuffs, IVs, or blood draws on restricted arm).
steps.ref: Health → Chronic / critical illness & ER care

steps.t: Grab the hospital go-bag & log every update
steps.d: Bring phone + long charger, typed medication list, rescue meds, insurance card, button-up shirt, and lip balm. Log doctors' names and instructions in the Call & claim log.

steps.t: Appoint a Communication Captain & Care Squad
steps.d: Pick one trusted friend or relative to post updates so neither of you repeats draining news 20 times. Delegate rides, school runs, groceries, and meals.

steps.t: Ask for a hospital social worker, palliative care & financial aid
steps.d: Social workers unlock free parking passes, gas cards, meal vouchers, charity care, and manufacturer drug copay cards. Palliative care relieves pain, nausea, and fatigue during active treatment (it is not hospice).

steps.t: Cross-check every hospital bill against the Insurance EOB
steps.d: Wait until your insurer's Explanation of Benefits (EOB) settles before paying provider bills so you catch duplicate charges, coding errors, and prior-auth denials.

steps.t: Protect the caregiver & kids
steps.d: Give kids' teachers and school counselors an early heads-up so they watch for quiet stress, enforce germ/visitor boundaries, and accept respite help without guilt.

steps.t: Commit to a 6-to-12 month 'No Big Decisions' freeze
steps.d: Grief and stress make big financial choices risky. Do not buy or sell a house, buy a luxury car, invest in anyone's business, or lend large sums right away.
steps.ref: Money → Beginner's guide: handling big money

steps.t: Tell almost nobody the payout amount
steps.d: Privacy protects you from relatives asking for loans, pushy salespeople, and bereavement scammers.

steps.t: Park the payout safely under bank deposit-insurance limits
steps.d: Do not leave $1M sitting in one checking account. Split across government-insured High-Yield Savings Accounts or short-term Treasury money market/bills, and check interest rates before leaving it in an insurer's 'retained asset' checkbook.
steps.ref: Money → Beginner's guide: handling big money

steps.t: Set up an automatic 'Monthly Paycheck' to checking
steps.d: Auto-transfer only your usual monthly spending from savings into checking each month so household bills run calmly without dipping impulsively into the lump sum.
steps.ref: Money → My instructions for big money / insurance payouts
steps.refBlock: My instructions for big money / insurance payouts

steps.t: Only pay high-interest joint debts; hold off on everything else
steps.d: Pay off high-interest joint credit cards (>10%). Wait before paying off a low-rate mortgage, and never pay solo unsecured debts solely in the deceased's name until our estate attorney reviews them.

steps.t: Talk to a CPA/tax advisor before selling investments or a home
steps.d: Life insurance payouts are usually income-tax-free, and inherited assets often get a 'step-up in cost basis.' Ask about surviving-spouse tax status before triggering capital gains.

phases.when: Months 6 to 12 — Hire Safe Help & Build a Plan

steps.t: Only hire a Fee-Only Fiduciary advisor (zero commissions)
steps.d: Pay by the hour or flat annual fee—never commission. Walk out immediately if anyone pitches whole/indexed life insurance, variable annuities, ULIPs, or 'expires this Friday' deals.
steps.ref: Money → Beginner's guide: handling big money

steps.t: Divide the money into 4 clear buckets
steps.d: Keep 12 months in cash, pay high-interest joint debt, set aside 1–5 year needs in safe short-term instruments, and invest the rest in a simple low-cost diversified portfolio using a ~3.5%–4% annual withdrawal rule.
steps.ref: Money → Beginner's guide: handling big money

steps.t: Follow a simple 15-minute monthly money routine
steps.d: Check your checking buffer, keep credit cards on full-statement autopay, drop tax letters into one folder, and meet your fee-only advisor once a year.

steps.t: Update your own beneficiaries, will & kids' guardian
steps.d: Ensure your new accounts, insurance, and estate documents reflect your updated wishes.

SCRIPTS: Calling a bank or insurer
"I'm calling about my spouse's account. They are [in the hospital / have passed away]. I have [power of attorney / a death certificate]. What do you need from me, and can you send it in writing?"
Calling an immigration attorney about dependent status

"My spouse is on [H-1B / L-1 / work visa] and [is hospitalized / lost their job / has passed away]. I am on [H-4 / dependent status] and our pending filings are [I-140 / I-485 / none]. What are our exact deadlines and options before we make any travel or filing moves?"
When someone pushes you to decide
"I'm not making any decisions right now. Please send me the details and I'll get back to you."
When a debt collector calls about a solo debt
"This account was solely in my spouse's name. Please send all documentation in writing to the estate, and I will have our attorney review it."
Asking a friend for help
"Could you take over [meals / school runs / phone calls] this week? It would help me a lot."
Telling the kids
"Something hard happened. You are safe and you are loved, and we'll take care of each other. You can ask me anything."
Setting visitor, germ & energy boundaries

"Thank you so much for wanting to visit. Right now our medical team needs us to avoid anyone with even mild sniffles, strong scents, or surprise drop-ins. Text [Communication Captain] to schedule a short window on a good day."
Asking a hospital social worker for financial & practical aid

"We're navigating ongoing [diagnosis/treatment]. Could you connect us with hospital financial aid/charity care, manufacturer drug copay assistance, parking/gas/meal vouchers, palliative symptom support, and FMLA/disability paperwork help?"
Updating a child's teacher or school counselor

"Wanted to share privately that [child's name]'s parent is going through serious medical treatment right now. Things at home feel heavy—please let me or the counselor know if you notice any quiet withdrawal, tiredness, or anxiety at school."
Saying no to salespeople or relatives asking for money

"Our estate attorney and fee-only advisor have everything frozen in a waiting period for the next year, and I can't lend money, buy new policies, or sign any investments until they approve it in writing."

MONEY_GUIDE.title: 1. Rule #1: The 6-to-12 Month Freeze
MONEY_GUIDE.summary: If you have never managed money before and just received a large payout (like $1M), your single most powerful financial move is doing very little for 6 to 12 months while you heal.
bullets: Do NOT sell your home or buy a new house right away—renting or staying put for 1 year avoids costly mistakes.
Do NOT buy annuities, whole/indexed life insurance, crypto, timeshares, or invest in anyone's business.
Do NOT lend large sums to family or friends; once money leaves, it rarely comes back.
Keep all big-decision answers simple: "Our advisor has us in a 12-month freeze before we decide anything."

MONEY_GUIDE.title: 2. Where to Park a Big Payout Safely Today
MONEY_GUIDE.summary: Life insurance payouts are usually income-tax-free, but leaving $1,000,000 sitting in a single checking account is risky and earns near zero.
bullets: Watch deposit-insurance limits: never hold more than the government-insured cap in a single bank institution.
Beware the insurer's 'Retained Asset Account' (checkbook they mail you)—it often pays much lower interest and isn't always bank-insured; transfer funds to your own safe accounts.
Park cash safely in 2–4 insured High-Yield Savings Accounts or a government Treasury Money Market / short-term government bills while you pause.
Pay yourself a 'Monthly Paycheck': set an automatic monthly transfer from savings to your bill-pay checking account matching your usual monthly budget so daily life stays calm.

MONEY_GUIDE.title: 3. The 4-Bucket Plan (How to Allocate $1,000,000)
MONEY_GUIDE.summary: Think of a lump sum as four simple jars—never one giant pile to spend down:
bullets: Bucket 1 — 12-Month Safety Cash (10%–15% / ~$100k–$150k): Covers 1 full year of bills in insured High-Yield Savings so you never panic if something breaks.

Bucket 2 — High-Interest Joint Debt Only (0%–10%): Pay off joint credit cards (>10%). Do NOT rush to pay off a 3%–5% mortgage, and ask our attorney before paying any solo debt only in the deceased's name.
Bucket 3 — Near-Term 1–5 Year Goals (10%–15% / ~$100k–$150k): Upcoming tuition, reliable car replacement, or medical buffer in safe CDs, Treasury bills, or short-term government bonds.
Bucket 4 — Long-Term Income Engine (60%–75% / ~$600k–$750k): Broad low-cost index funds managed with a fee-only advisor so it grows faster than inflation.
MONEY_GUIDE.note: The ~3.5%–4% Rule: Every $100,000 invested long-term can sustainably pay about $3,500–$4,000 per year (~$290–$330/mo) for 30+ years without running out. At 4%, $750,000 generates ~$30,000/yr ($2,500/mo) — and $1,000,000 generates ~$40,000/yr ($3,333/mo) — alongside survivor pensions or your own income. General education only, not personal financial advice.

MONEY_GUIDE.title: 4. How to Hire Help Without Getting Ripped Off
MONEY_GUIDE.summary: Grieving survivors are the #1 target of commission-based salespeople posing as 'advisors.' Hire slowly and verify credentials in writing.
bullets: ONLY hire a Fee-Only Fiduciary (paid a flat project fee, hourly rate, or transparent flat annual fee—zero product commissions).
Walk away immediately from: Whole/Indexed Universal Life insurance (IUL), Variable Annuities with 7-year surrender fees, ULIPs, or anyone saying 'sign before Friday.'

Ask these 3 exact questions before hiring anyone: (1) 'Will you sign a written Fiduciary Oath putting my interests first 100% of the time?' (2) 'Do you earn ANY commission, kickback, or referral fee from products you recommend?' (3) 'What is your total all-in dollar fee per year?'

MONEY_GUIDE.title: 5. Protecting Yourself From Relatives & Scammers
MONEY_GUIDE.summary: Keep the payout size strictly private. Even kind relatives make bad assumptions when they hear a big number.
bullets: Never tell extended family, neighbors, or social media how much insurance paid out.

Watch out for the 4 classic bereavement scams: (1) fake overdue funeral/cremation invoices, (2) callers claiming unpaid deceased taxes demanding immediate wire/Zelle/UPI/gift cards, (3) fake 'urgent' collectors for solo credit cards, and (4) sudden 'investment mentors' or romance contacts.
Keep a simple safety rule: NEVER wire money, buy gift cards, or approve crypto transfers under phone urgency. Hang up and verify independently.

MONEY_GUIDE.title: 6. Your 15-Minute Monthly Money Routine
MONEY_GUIDE.summary: If you have never managed household bills before, this simple checklist keeps everything running smoothly:
bullets: Keep ~1.5x your normal monthly budget in your bill-pay checking account; auto-transfer the same 'paycheck' from savings once a month.
Put credit cards on autopay for the FULL statement balance (never just minimum) so you pay $0 interest.
Create one folder (physical + digital) called 'Tax Letters This Year' and drop every 1099 / W-2 / Form 16 / receipt into it.
Before selling any stocks, mutual funds, or real estate, ask a CPA about 'Step-Up in Cost Basis' and Surviving Spouse tax rules—selling too fast can trigger unnecessary taxes.

PRO_FINDER.title: 1. Estate & Probate Attorney (Even Without a Will)
PRO_FINDER.summary: You don't need to be wealthy—or have an existing lawyer—to get trustworthy estate or probate help affordably.
bullets: Check hidden employer perks first: an Employee Assistance Program (EAP) often includes a free 30-minute legal consult, and Group Legal Plans (e.g., MetLife Legal / ARAG) cover wills & POA for a low payroll fee.
Use your official State or National Bar Association Lawyer Referral Service (free or $25–$50 for a 30-minute consult) or local Legal Aid / law school elder-law clinics for free/sliding-scale help.
In civil-law countries (much of Europe), a public Notary handles wills and succession directly under fixed government fee schedules.
Free steps you can do today: sign free hospital/state Advance Healthcare Directive forms and add free POD/TOD ('Payable/Transferable on Death') beneficiaries on bank and investment accounts.
PRO_FINDER.note: First question to ask: "Do you offer a free or flat-fee initial consult, and can you quote a flat fee for will/POA drafting or probate administration?"

PRO_FINDER.title: 2. Immigration Attorney (Visas, Dependents & Cross-Border)
PRO_FINDER.summary: Company immigration lawyers represent the employer, not solely your family—know how to get independent, vetted help quickly.
bullets: Ask HR/company immigration counsel immediately for PDF copies of all filings (I-797, I-140, PERM, I-485, work permits) so an independent lawyer can review your exact timeline.
Book a 30–60 minute independent strategy consult ($150–$350) through official directories (AILA in US, IAA/OISC or Law Society in UK, CICC in Canada, OMARA in Australia) BEFORE leaving the country.

Need free or low-cost help? Search DOJ-accredited nonprofit clinics (e.g., ImmigrationLawHelp.org in the US), law school immigration clinics, and your home-country Embassy/Consulate for emergency travel/repatriation letters.
PRO_FINDER.note: Red flag: NEVER pay an unlicensed 'notario', travel agent, or social-media 'visa consultant.' Always verify their active bar number or government regulator ID.

PRO_FINDER.title: 3. Financial Advisor (No Large Portfolio Required)
PRO_FINDER.summary: You do not need $500k+ to get good financial advice—and you never have to buy an insurance product or give up a % of your savings.
bullets: Free starting points: Employer EAP financial coaching, nonprofit credit counseling (NFCC / MoneyHelper / National Debt Helpline), and pro-bono CFP® programs (like Foundation for Financial Planning for families facing serious illness or bereavement).

Pay only for advice, never sales: look for Hourly or Flat-Fee Advice-Only / Fee-Only Fiduciaries (Garrett Planning Network, AdviceOnlyNetwork, NAPFA, XYPN in US; SEBI-RIA & feeonlyindia.com in India; Chartered IFA in UK).
Need a calm DIY option while pausing? A single low-cost broad Target-Date or Balanced Index Fund at a major low-cost brokerage beats expensive managed accounts or annuities.
PRO_FINDER.note: Red flag: 'Free' advisors at banks or insurance agencies usually earn large commissions selling annuities, whole/indexed life insurance, or ULIPs. Always demand a written Fiduciary Oath.

PRO_FINDER.title: 4. Tax Consultant / CPA / Chartered Accountant (CA)
PRO_FINDER.summary: Use free volunteer tax clinics for routine returns, or hire a licensed tax pro for a one-time crisis/estate tax session.
bullets: Free official help for straightforward returns: IRS VITA / TCE and AARP Tax-Aide (US), CVITP (Canada), ATO Tax Help (Australia), and TaxAid (UK).

For final returns, surviving-spouse filing rules, inherited property/stocks, or insurance questions: hire an independent CPA / Enrolled Agent (EA) / Chartered Accountant (CA) for a one-time hourly/flat return.
Cross-border / NRI families (e.g., US + India): specifically ask for a cross-border CPA/CA experienced with FBAR, FATCA (Form 8938), Form 3520, and Double Taxation Treaties (DTAA).
PRO_FINDER.note: Ask before selling inherited assets: "How do surviving-spouse tax rules and step-up in cost basis affect what I would owe if I sell?"

PRO_FINDER.title: 5. Free 'Hidden Allies' Almost Every Family Forgets
PRO_FINDER.summary: Before spending savings on private consultants, tap free institutional advocates who handle these crises every day.
bullets: Hospital Social Worker & Patient Navigator (free): ask at admission or clinic for charity care applications, drug copay cards, parking/gas/meal vouchers, rehab placement, and FMLA/disability forms.
Employer EAP (free for the whole household): covers grief counseling, short legal consults, financial coaching, and childcare/eldercare referrals—even after work hours.

Nonprofit Medical Bill & Illness Advocates (free): Dollar For (helps cancel eligible nonprofit hospital bills via charity care), Patient Advocate Foundation (free case managers), and national disease foundations.
Home-Country Consulate & School Counselors: consulates help with overseas documents and travel emergencies; school counselors quietly support children during illness or loss.
PRO_FINDER.note: You don't need to assemble a whole team in one week—make just ONE free call (EAP, hospital social worker, or bar referral) to get steady next steps.
